Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Common symptoms of diabetes include: increased urination; feeling very thirsty; feeling very hungry, even after you have eaten; blurred vision; fatigue; sores that do not heal; frequent infections, such as urinary tract infections, skin infections, or yeast infections. [1]
- In addition to the common symptoms of diabetes listed above, people may find out they have type 2 diabetes when they develop symptoms of other health problems from diabetes. [2]
- In addition to some of the common diabetes symptoms listed above, people with type 1 diabetes may also have an unexplained weight loss. [3]
- Common symptoms of type diabetes in children include: having to urinate more often; eating more but losing weight; feeling very thirsty. [3]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- These symptoms are less common in adults with type 1 diabetes. [1]
- For some adults, symptoms of type 1 diabetes may develop slowly and seem more like type 2 diabetes. [1]
- Sometimes, people find out they have type 1 diabetes when they have signs and symptoms of a condition called diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). [1]
- Most often, ketoacidosis affects people with type 1 diabetes. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Symptoms of type 2 diabetes can develop slowly, over several years. [1]
- Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms, or symptoms can be so mild that people might not even notice them. [1]
- In addition to the common symptoms of diabetes listed above, people may find out they have type 2 diabetes when they develop symptoms of other health problems from diabetes. [1]
- In type 2 diabetes, the symptoms can be mild and may take many years to be noticed. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Children and teens are also at higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes if, in addition to the previous risk factors, they were born with a low birth weight or if their parent had gestational diabetes while pregnant with the child. [1]
- You can also take the Diabetes Risk Test to learn more about your risk for type 2 diabetes. [1]
- Your chances of developing type 2 diabetes depend on a combination of risk factors. [3]
- Read about risk factors for type 2 diabetes below, and see which ones apply to you. [3]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Lifestyle changes are the best way to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes. [2]
- To help prevent type 2 diabetes and its complications, people should: reach and keep a health body weight; stay physically active with at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise each week; eat a healthy diet and avoid sugar and saturated fat; not smoke tobacco. [2]
- You can help prevent or delay type 2 diabetes by losing a modest amount of weight by following a reduced-calorie eating plan and being physically active most days of the week. [3]
- Ask your doctor if you should take the diabetes drug metformin to help prevent or delay type 2 diabetes. [3]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- About 1 in 3 Americans has prediabetes, according to recent diabetes statistics from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. [1]
- You won’t know if you have prediabetes unless you are tested. [1]
- If you have prediabetes, you can lower your chance of developing type 2 diabetes. [1]
- If you have prediabetes, you can lower your chance of developing type 2 diabetes. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- The A1C test shows your average blood glucose level over the last 3 months. [1]
- Your A1C goal may be different if you have other health problems. [1]
- Ask your health care team how often you should have the test and what your goal should be. [1]
- You do not get the same level of detail from blood tests—such as the A1C test—that you take at a health care professional’s office. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Some people with diabetes have a blood pressure goal below 130/80 mm Hg. [1]
- Your recommended blood pressure goal may depend on what other health conditions you have. [2]
- Blood pressure goal is less than 130/80 if you have: cardiovascular disease (heart disease or stroke); diabetes (high blood sugar); chronic kidney disease; high risk for cardiovascular disease. [2]
- For most people, the goal is to have a blood pressure less than 140/90. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- The diabetes ABCs can help you manage your blood glucose, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels. [1]
- Managing your ABCs may lower your chances of having health problems from diabetes, such as a heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, blindness, and foot or leg amputations. [1]
- For most people with diabetes, their goal is an A1C level below 7%. [2]
- If you have heart disease or are at high risk for diabetes health problems, your goal may be lower. [3]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Physical activity may help you lower blood glucose, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels. [1]
- Try to get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity, such as brisk walking, each week. [1]
- If you often have low blood glucose levels, you may need to change your diabetes meal plan, physical activity plan, or medicines. [4]
- Diabetes can be treated with diet, physical activity and medication, and its consequences avoided through regular screening for complications and timely treatment. [5]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Another way to estimate your risk of developing diabetes is to measure your waist circumference. [1]
- Men have a higher risk of developing diabetes if their waist circumference is more than 40 inches, while women who are not pregnant have a higher risk if their waist circumference is more than 35 inches. [1]
- Having a large waist circumference is a risk factor for diabetes and heart disease, even if you have a normal BMI. [1]
- To see if your weight may put you at risk for type 2 diabetes, learn your body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Type 1 diabetes develops when the body’s immune system destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin. [1]
- Genes and factors in the environment—the places where people live, play, work, study, and gather—may trigger the immune system to destroy beta cells in type 1 diabetes. [1]
- Studies such as The Environmental Determinants of Diabetes in the Young (TEDDY) are trying to learn more about the causes of type 1 diabetes. [2]
- Type 1 Diabetes TrialNet and other groups are working to find treatments that may prevent or slow the development of type 1 diabetes in people who are at risk for getting the disease. [2]

- You have type 2 diabetes when health care professionals diagnose your blood glucose level as being too high. [1]
- Researchers don’t fully know what causes problems with insulin production and insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes. [1]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- If you take medicines for these conditions, you may want to ask your primary health care professional if your medicines could affect your risk of developing diabetes. [2]
- Some people with type 2 diabetes will need to take medicines to help manage their blood sugar levels. [3]
- Along with medicines to lower blood sugar, people with diabetes often need medications to lower their blood pressure and statins to reduce the risk of complications. [3]
- Along with medicines to lower blood sugar, people with diabetes often need medications to lower their blood pressure and statins to reduce the risk of complications. [4]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Many factors raise your risk of high blood pressure. [1]
- A healthy lifestyle can lower your risk for developing high blood pressure. [1]
- But, you can still take steps to reduce your risk of high blood pressure and its complications. [1]
- Research shows that factors such as income, education level, where you live, and the type of job you have, as well as stressors on the job may raise your risk of high blood pressure. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Lifestyle changes can help lower high blood pressure and can help anyone with hypertension. [1]
- These lifestyle changes can help prevent and lower high blood pressure. [1]
- Lifestyle changes can help lower high blood pressure. [2]
- The combination of medicines and heart-healthy lifestyle changes can help control and lower your high blood pressure and prevent heart disease. [3]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Hypertension is diagnosed if, when it is measured on two different days, the systolic blood pressure readings on both days is ≥140 mmHg and/or the diastolic blood pressure readings on both days is ≥90 mmHg. [1]
- The only way to detect hypertension is to have a health professional measure blood pressure. [2]
- Hypertension (high blood pressure) is when the pressure in your blood vessels is too high (140/90 mmHg or higher). [3]
- An estimated 1.4 billion adults aged 30–79 years worldwide had hypertension in 2024; this represents 33% of the popluation in this age range: Two-thirds of adults aged 30–79 years who have hypertension live in low- and middle-income countries; An estimated 600 million adults with hypertension (44%) are unaware that they have the condition; Approximately 630 million adults with hypertension (44%) are diagnosed and treated; Approximately 320 million adults with hypertension (23%) have it under control; Hypertension is a major cause of premature death worldwide; One of the global targets for noncommunicable diseases is to reduce the prevalence of uncontrolled hypertension by 25% between 2010 and 2025. [4]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Very high blood pressures can cause headaches, blurred vision, chest pain and other symptoms. [1]
- People with very high blood pressure (usually 180/120 or higher) can experience symptoms including: severe headaches; chest pain; dizziness; difficulty breathing; nausea; vomiting; blurred vision or other vision changes; anxiety; confusion; buzzing in the ears; nosebleeds; abnormal heart rhythm. [1]
- If you are experiencing any of these symptoms and a high blood pressure, seek care immediately. [1]
- People with high blood pressure may not feel symptoms. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Among other complications, hypertension can cause serious damage to the heart. [1]
- In addition, hypertension can cause kidney damage, leading to kidney failure. [1]
- If hypertension isn’t treated, it can cause other health conditions like kidney disease, heart disease and stroke. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- If you have high blood pressure, your provider may recommend that you adopt a heart-healthy lifestyle to help lower and control high blood pressure: Choose heart-healthy foods such as those in the DASH eating plan. [1]
- NHLBI-funded research has shown that DASH combined with a low-salt eating plan can be as effective as medicines in lowering high blood pressure. [1]
- Living With the DASH Eating Plan and Tips to Reduce Salt and Sodium offer more information. [1]
- For more ways to limit your sodium, visit the DASH Eating Plan page or print out the Tips to Reduce Salt and Sodium handout; Avoid or limit alcohol; Get regular physical activity. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- There are several common high blood pressure medicines your provider can prescribe: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors keep your blood vessels from narrowing as much; Angiotensin II receptor blockers also keep blood vessels from narrowing; Calcium channel blockers prevent calcium from entering the muscle cells of your heart and blood vessels. [1]
- The main diuretic for high blood pressure treatment is thiazide. [1]
- Diuretics are often used with other high blood pressure medicines, sometimes in one combined pill. [1]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- The recommended amount for adults is 7 to 9 hours of sleep per day. [1]
- Children and adolescents may need more sleep. [2]
- Not getting enough quality sleep, including waking up often throughout the night, may raise your risk of coronary heart disease. [3]
- While you sleep, your heart does not work as hard as it does when you are awake. [3]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- If you are having a heart attack, you may experience one or more of the symptoms below: Chest pain, heaviness, or discomfort in the center or left side of the chest (this is the most common symptom); Pain or discomfort in one or both arms, your back, shoulders, neck, jaw, or above your belly button; Shortness of breath when resting or doing a little bit of physical activity (this is more common in older adults); Sweating a lot for no reason; Feeling unusually tired for no reason, sometimes for days (this is more common in women); Nausea (feeling sick to the stomach) and vomiting; Light-headedness or sudden dizziness; Rapid or irregular heartbeat. [1]
- It is also possible to have mild symptoms or even no symptoms at all and still have a heart attack. [1]
- The symptoms of a heart attack can be different from person to person and different between men and women. [2]
- If you’ve already had a heart attack, your symptoms may not be the same for another one. [2]

Most relevant statements from the documents:
- Knowing the difference between stable angina (chest pain in people who have coronary artery disease) and a heart attack is important: The pain from angina usually happens after physical activity and goes away in a few minutes when you rest or take medicine to treat it; The pain from a heart attack is more serious than the pain from angina. [1]
- If you don’t know whether your chest pain is angina or a heart attack, call 9-1-1. [1]
- Not all heart attacks begin with the sudden and crushing chest pain that comes when the blood flow to heart gets blocked. [4]
